title: Health access is improving globally, but essential-service gaps and care costs still convert illness into household insecurity
source_unit: WHO and World Bank, Tracking Universal Health Coverage: 2025 Global Monitoring Report
geography: 195 countries or territories for service coverage; 168 countries for financial hardship time series

observations.period: 2000-2023; latest service-coverage estimate reported in the 2025 edition

denominator.unit: countries or territories represented in the revised service-coverage time series

service_coverage_index_2000.unit: global UHC service-coverage index points in 2000

service_coverage_index_2023.unit: global UHC service-coverage index points in 2023

people_lacking_essential_service_coverag.unit: people estimated to lack coverage for essential health services in 2023

observations.method: The report uses the revised SDG 3.8.1 UHC service-coverage index, a composite of 14 tracer indicators spanning reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health; infectious diseases; noncommunicable diseases; and service capacity and access.
observations.uncertainty: The index summarizes selected service dimensions and does not equal effective, timely, high-quality care for every person. The global population estimate is derived from the index and should not be read as a count of untreated illness or unmet need for every service.
observations.subgroup: People seeking essential health services, health systems, governments, and communities across income levels and regions.
observations.counterinterpretation: The index rose substantially since 2000, showing broad system gains; remaining gaps may reflect different service mixes and measurement limits as well as absolute access failures.

observations.period: 2000-2022; latest financial-hardship estimate reported in the 2025 edition

denominator.unit: countries with primary time-series data represented in the financial-hardship analysis

financial_hardship_share_2000.unit: percent of the population experiencing large or impoverishing out-of-pocket health-payment hardship in 2000

financial_hardship_share_2022.unit: percent of the population experiencing large or impoverishing out-of-pocket health-payment hardship in 2022

people_financial_hardship_2022.unit: people estimated to experience financial hardship due to out-of-pocket health spending in 2022

observations.method: The revised SDG 3.8.2 measure identifies out-of-pocket health spending exceeding 40% of a household's discretionary budget, with hardship including spending that is impoverishing or substantially reduces the ability to consume other goods and services.
observations.uncertainty: The estimate is not a measure of medical debt alone and does not identify which care, medicine, insurance, income, or policy pathway produced hardship. Reference years differ between service coverage and financial protection.
observations.subgroup: Households paying out of pocket for health care, especially households near poverty or with limited discretionary consumption capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: The global hardship share declined from 2000 to 2022 even while the absolute burden remains very large; broader public financing and targeted protection can improve affordability without eliminating all care-related household tradeoffs.

boundary: This record adds global public-system coverage and household financial-protection evidence. It is not respondent-level data, does not estimate individual treatment effects, and does not establish that coverage gaps or out-of-pocket spending caused any specific consumer, health, work, or political outcome.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: WHO/World Bank UHC Global Monitoring Report 2025 PDF and official WHO publication/news pages retrieved; service-coverage and financial-hardship values cross-checked against the official release.
